title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers used AI-generated images and videos to impersonate a real, named immigration attorney across social media platforms, creating hundreds of fake profiles to sell fraudulent legal services to immigrants. The failure here is impersonation: generative AI tools were used outside any legitimate deployment context, as instruments of fraud rather than products gone wrong in normal use. The scheme operated entirely through social media, WhatsApp, and digital payment apps, with no human verification step between a fake profile and a victim's payment.

The vulnerability exploited was the absence of identity checks on the platforms hosting the fake profiles. Nearly 6,500 profiles were removed only after the real attorney hired a private anti-piracy company to find and report them, meaning the platforms did not catch the impersonation at scale on their own. Catching this earlier would have required either automated detection of synthetic media at the point of upload or a mechanism for verifying that accounts offering professional services belong to licensed practitioners.

It is not established who is responsible for creating the fake profiles, where they are located, or whether any law enforcement action has produced findings or charges.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles featuring AI-generated images of Leal, falsely offering immigration services like US residency assistance for fees ranging around $2,200. The scams typically direct people through social media to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, where fraudsters send phony contracts and collect payments through digital payment apps like Venmo and Zelle.

Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and intensified over the past three months. An anti-piracy company he hired has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the source of the fraud. He is warning immigrants to verify anyone offering immigration services online and to be cautious of social media advertisements demanding upfront payment.
